land_owner.value: The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
land_owner.note: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (`e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson`), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land_sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE ROOF IS AN INVENTION AND THIS CANNOT OUTRANK IT. The footprint stands 10 m inside the tract's nearest boundary, which on a documented building would carry the middle tier, but this building was dealt to its lot by a recipe and is not there. The tract is real and the register's words about it are read; what is graded here is the claim that THIS roof stands on it, and that claim is the recipe's. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

persons.name: Jos. Britton
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Jos. Britton' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 28 January 1834, column 1 — dated 1834-01-28. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). persons.name: Henry Moore
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'HENRY MOORE' and 'HUNKY MOOR)' and 'Hees Moone' and 'Henry Moore, Faq,' and 'Hiway Meoue' and 'RENRY MOORE,' and 'Y MOORE' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the American of 4 July 1835, column 1; the American of 11 July 1835, column 1; the American of 22 August 1835, column 5; the Democrat of 4 June 1835, column 5; the Democrat of 24 June 1835, column 10; the Democrat of 5 August 1835, column 18, and 1 further mention(s). The corpus associates the name with Chicago, J. H. Kinzie's new store; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `attorney` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Moore, Mrs. Harriet M. | Letter. | December 30, 1891.” (second_presb_0256, printed page 168), admitted 1891-12-30 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Moore' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins H. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

NOBODY HERE IS NAMED BY ANY SOURCE. The 1840 Chicago schedule counts children under ten at 27% of the town and women of twenty to twenty-nine as its second-largest band; the 1835 layer the sources can name holds 15 women, because the rolls that name this town — a letter list, a voters' roll, a subscription — print men. That gap is the shape of the evidence and not a reading of the town, so the order book counts it bucket by bucket and this household is drawn against those counts. Every value on it carries the model row and the seed that redraws it, and a source naming a woman who kept her own house in this division retires the whole record. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). This household is one of the surplus the re-cut HOLDS rather than retires: the owner's ruling of 2026-09-24 re-families it into a cell the book still orders instead of un-writing it, and `refamilied` above is the whole of what that changed.
